FARGO, North Dakota (CNN)  -- Forecasters issued flash flood warnings for Bismarck and surrounding areas Wednesday, as volunteers rushed to fill sandbags ahead of expected record floods in the flat state of North Dakota. Explosives are set off in the Missouri River on Wednesday to break up ice jams. Areas of three counties -- Morton, Emmons and Burleigh, which includes the North Dakota capital of Bismarck -- were under a flash flood warning until 12:30 p.m. CT (1:30 p.m. ET), the National Weather Service said. In an effort to alleviate the flooding, demolition crews blew up an ice jam Wednesday evening south of  Bismarck, according to CNN affiliate KXMB. Mayor John Warford said that water appeared to be moving more freely in the Missouri River after the explosives were set off, KXMB reported. The plan is make sure water continues flow through the river channel and not spread out over land. Ice jams in rivers have been a major factor in the flooding there. Most of the state, which endured a particularly harsh winter, remained under a flood warning Wednesday, with forecasters predicting possibly record flood levels on several rivers. Snow, which continued to fall Wednesday, complicated preparations, city officials said. "I woke up this morning and looked outside, I guess I thought of the same thing everybody else did. ... [What] came to mind is what a revolting development this is," said Mark Voxland, the mayor of Moorhead, Minnesota, a city just outside of Fargo.  Watch flooded fields of snow » . More than 1,000 people were evacuated from an area near Bismarck on Tuesday night as the Missouri River flooded, Rick Robinson of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services said Wednesday.  See a map of the affected area » . Emergency officials said they were particularly concerned about the Red River, which snakes through eastern portions of North and South Dakota and western Minnesota. The river is expected to crest between 39 and 41 feet in Fargo on Friday, according to Cecily Fong of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services. The record for the Red River at Fargo was set in 1897 at 40.1 feet, according to Pat Slattery of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The threat of flooding prompted authorities to ask for volunteers to fill sandbags either to build temporary dikes or to bolster existing ones. In some areas, even at 3:30 a.m., hundreds of volunteers packed into individual sandbagging centers, an organizer said.  See images of flooding, preparation » . "There have been so many volunteers that we had to turn people away," said Ryan McEwan, a supervisor at one volunteer coordinating center. "It is very busy. They are filling sandbags as fast as they can." As of late Tuesday, Fargo residents and out-of-town volunteers had filled more than 1 million sandbags out of the needed 2 million. Fargo Deputy Mayor Tim Mahoney said he hoped that goal would be met by Thursday. Fargo's mayor, Dennis Walaker, said Wednesday that his city was about 95 percent prepared for the flooding, which is expected later in the week. "I went and looked at the dikes this morning, and they're significant, absolutely significant," he said in a briefing Wednesday morning. However, he said, "We have some areas we need to shore up." Just south of Fargo, authorities said they had rescued several people in Oxbow, a town of about 238 people, after a residential dike gave way. In some places, water had reached halfway up residents' basement stairs, and in others, it had reached the main level of homes, Sgt. Gail Wichmann said. CNN's Chris Welch contributed to this report.

FARGO, North Dakota (CNN) — On Wednesday, weather officials placed Bismarck and nearby communities under flash flood warnings while volunteers worked quickly to fill sandbags before what were expected to be historic floods across the flat terrain of North Dakota.

Crews used explosives Wednesday on the Missouri River to break apart ice jams. The National Weather Service said parts of Morton, Emmons and Burleigh counties — including Bismarck, the state capital — were under a flash flood warning until 12:30 p.m. CT, or 1:30 p.m. ET.

CNN affiliate KXMB reported that demolition teams detonated explosives Wednesday evening south of Bismarck to help reduce flooding by clearing an ice blockage. Bismarck Mayor John Warford said afterward that the Missouri River seemed to be flowing more freely, according to KXMB. The goal was to keep water moving within the river channel rather than spilling across surrounding land.

Ice jams on rivers have played a significant role in the flooding in the area. Much of North Dakota, which had gone through an especially severe winter, remained under flood warnings Wednesday. Forecasters said several rivers could reach record levels. City officials also said ongoing snowfall Wednesday made preparations more difficult.

Mark Voxland, mayor of Moorhead, Minnesota — located just outside Fargo — described waking up to the snow and thinking what many others likely thought: “What a revolting development this is.”

More than 1,000 residents were evacuated Tuesday night from an area near Bismarck after the Missouri River flooded, Rick Robinson of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services said Wednesday.

Emergency management officials said one of their biggest concerns was the Red River, which winds through eastern North and South Dakota and western Minnesota. Cecily Fong of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services said the river was expected to crest in Fargo on Friday between 39 and 41 feet. According to Pat Slattery of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Red River’s record level at Fargo was 40.1 feet, set in 1897.

Because of the flood risk, officials called on volunteers to fill sandbags for use in constructing temporary dikes or strengthening existing barriers. One organizer said that in some locations, hundreds of people were already gathered at sandbagging sites as early as 3:30 a.m.

“There have been so many volunteers that we had to turn people away,” said Ryan McEwan, a supervisor at a volunteer coordination center. “It is very busy. They are filling sandbags as fast as they can.”

By late Tuesday, Fargo residents and volunteers from outside the city had filled more than 1 million sandbags, out of the 2 million needed. Deputy Mayor Tim Mahoney said he hoped the full target would be reached by Thursday.

Fargo Mayor Dennis Walaker said Wednesday that the city was roughly 95 percent ready for the flooding expected later in the week. During a Wednesday morning briefing, he said he had inspected the dikes and found them to be “significant, absolutely significant.” Still, he added that some areas still needed reinforcement.

South of Fargo, officials said several people had been rescued in Oxbow, a town of about 238 residents, after a residential dike failed. Sgt. Gail Wichmann said that in some homes, floodwater had risen halfway up basement staircases, while in others it had reached the main floor.

CNN’s Chris Welch contributed to this report.

The National Weather Service issued flood warnings for portions of eastern North Dakota and western Minnesota, including communities along the Red River and its tributaries, warning that rapid snowmelt, recent rainfall and thick river ice were creating dangerous and unpredictable conditions. Forecasters cautioned that ice jams could cause water levels to rise suddenly, even in areas where gauges had not yet reached major flood stage.

“Flooding in this region can change quickly, especially when ice is involved,” the weather service said in its warning. “Residents should not drive through flooded roads and should be prepared to move to higher ground if conditions worsen.”

In Fargo, city crews and volunteers worked through cold winds and muddy conditions to fill and place sandbags along vulnerable stretches near homes, storm drains and low-lying roads. Emergency managers said thousands of sandbags had been prepared as officials monitored river forecasts and inspected temporary levees.

“This is exactly why we prepare early,” Fargo Mayor Tim Mahoney said at an afternoon briefing. “The river gives us some warning, but ice jams don’t always give us much. We’re asking residents to stay alert, help their neighbors and follow instructions from emergency crews.”

Officials said volunteers reported to sandbag sites throughout the day, including students, church groups, business employees and residents from across Cass County. Some teams filled bags, while others loaded pallets onto trucks headed for neighborhoods most at risk.

Cass County emergency officials said the volunteer response had been crucial.

“We can move a lot faster when the community shows up like this,” said Cass County Emergency Manager Jason Benson. “Every sandbag placed now gives us more time and more protection if the river rises overnight.”

Elsewhere in the region, authorities used explosives to break up ice jams that were backing water into fields, roads and rural properties. Officials said the controlled blasts were carried out by trained personnel in coordination with law enforcement and emergency management agencies after ice buildups blocked the natural flow of water.

The use of explosives underscored the danger posed by thick March ice, which can form temporary dams and send water surging into areas that had appeared safe only hours earlier.

“These ice jams are one of the biggest wild cards we face,” a local public works official said. “You can have a river level that looks manageable, and then an ice blockage shifts or breaks and suddenly the water moves fast.”

Road closures were reported in low-lying areas, and authorities urged drivers to obey barricades. Emergency officials repeated the standard warning: “Turn around, don’t drown.” Even shallow floodwater can hide washed-out pavement, deep ditches or fast-moving currents.

In Fargo neighborhoods with a long memory of major Red River floods, residents said preparations felt familiar but still tense. Some homeowners moved valuables from basements, checked sump pumps and helped elderly neighbors build small sandbag walls near doors and window wells.

City officials said permanent flood-control improvements have reduced some risk, but temporary defenses remain necessary when spring melt coincides with rain, ice and frozen ground.

“We are better protected than we were years ago, but we are not immune,” Mahoney said. “This is still the Red River Valley, and spring flooding is something we take seriously.”

The National Weather Service said river levels would continue to be monitored closely over the next several days. More warnings or advisories could be issued depending on temperatures, precipitation and the movement of ice downstream.

Emergency managers encouraged residents to sign up for local alerts, avoid riverbanks and report flooding or ice-related hazards to authorities.

“This is a community effort,” Benson said. “If people stay informed, stay out of dangerous areas and keep helping where they can, we’ll get through this together.”

The message to residents is simple: take the forecast seriously and follow evacuation guidance when it comes.”

Cass County officials said emergency operations centers are coordinating with local fire departments, sheriff’s deputies, the National Weather Service and state agencies. Crews have been monitoring levees around the clock, looking for seepage, slumping or overtopping.

“We have teams staged with boats, pumps and high-clearance vehicles,” said **Mark Ellingson**, Cass County’s director of emergency management. “Our biggest concern is complacency. If water is covering a road, do not drive through it. Conditions can change within minutes.”

### Volunteer sandbag lines stretch for blocks

Across the Fargo area, residents bundled in winter coats and rubber boots formed long lines to pass sandbags hand to hand. High school students, church groups, college athletes and retirees worked shoulder to shoulder as pallets of empty bags were filled, tied and loaded onto trucks.

At one sandbagging site, volunteers said they had been working in shifts since before sunrise.

“We’ve been through floods before, and everybody knows somebody who needs help,” said **Megan Sorenson**, a Fargo resident who came with her two teenage sons. “You don’t wait until the water is at the door. You show up early, and you keep going.”

Local officials said volunteers are being directed to priority locations rather than self-deploying, in part to keep traffic lanes clear for emergency vehicles.

“We need people, but we need them in the right places,” Ellingson said. “The coordination matters. One misplaced line of sandbags can redirect water into someone else’s neighborhood.”

### Rescue operations in Oxbow

In Oxbow, where floodwaters spread over low-lying roads and fields, authorities said several households were contacted after water began rising faster than expected. Firefighters and rescue personnel moved through neighborhoods in boats and amphibious vehicles, checking on residents who had chosen to stay.

One rescue crew helped evacuate an elderly couple after water surrounded their home and began reaching the garage, officials said. Another team delivered medication to a resident who was sheltering in place on the second floor of a home.

“We’re asking people not to wait until it becomes a rescue,” said **Oxbow Fire Chief Daniel Reeves**. “If an evacuation notice is issued, it is because access may be cut off. Once the water gets moving, even familiar roads become dangerous.”

Video from the area showed water lapping against mailboxes and covering stretches of rural roadway. In some neighborhoods, residents used sump pumps and makeshift barriers in an effort to keep basements dry.

State emergency officials said the North Dakota National Guard was on standby to assist with additional evacuations, aerial reconnaissance and flood barrier operations if local resources become overwhelmed.

### Harsh winter set the stage

The flood threat follows a punishing winter across the Northern Plains, where repeated storms buried communities under heavy snow and strong winds created deep drifts. Prolonged cold kept much of the snowpack intact well into spring.

Then, a shift toward warmer temperatures triggered rapid melting. In some areas, officials said snow that had accumulated for months began releasing water in just days.

NOAA data showed snow-water content across portions of the Red River Basin running above normal for the season, with some tributary basins holding enough water to produce significant runoff even without additional rain.

“Snow depth alone doesn’t tell the full story,” Mitchell said. “What matters is how much water is locked in that snow and how quickly it comes out. This year, the amount of water available for runoff is a major driver of the flood forecast.”

### Shelters open as roads close

Emergency shelters have opened in several communities for residents displaced by rising water or concerned about losing access to power, heat or medical care. Officials urged residents to pack emergency kits with medications, identification, phone chargers, pet supplies and important documents.

Road closures were increasing Tuesday night across Cass County and neighboring areas. Transportation officials warned that rural routes may become impassable quickly as water spreads across flat farmland.

“If you encounter water over the roadway, turn around,” the North Dakota Department of Transportation said in an advisory. “The road surface may be damaged or washed out beneath the water.”

Power crews were also monitoring substations and utility corridors in flood-prone areas. Officials said outages were possible if floodwaters reach electrical infrastructure.

### Record levels possible

While exact crest levels remained uncertain, forecasters said some river gauges could challenge records if warm weather continues and rain falls over the basin.

The Red River has a long history of destructive flooding, including major events that forced large-scale evacuations and caused extensive property damage. Local leaders said investments in permanent flood protection have improved the region’s resilience, but not every neighborhood is protected equally.

“We are better prepared than we were years ago, but prepared does not mean invulnerable,” Mayor Petersen said. “Every flood is different, and this one still has a lot of uncertainty.”

Officials emphasized that the most dangerous period may come as rivers crest and remain high, placing pressure on levees and temporary barriers.

“A flood fight is not over when the river stops rising,” Ellingson said. “You still have to hold the line.”

### ‘Everybody is watching the water’

As night fell, floodlights illuminated sandbag walls in neighborhoods along the river. Volunteers continued to fill bags while emergency vehicles moved between checkpoints.

In Oxbow, residents who evacuated waited for updates from officials, unsure when they would be able to return home.

“We’ve done everything we can do,” one resident, **Paul Erickson**, said after leaving his home with his family and two dogs. “Now everybody is watching the water.”

Forecasters said they would continue updating river projections as new temperature, precipitation and snowmelt data come in. Emergency officials urged residents to monitor local alerts and be ready to move quickly if evacuation orders are issued.

“This is a serious flood threat,” Mitchell said. “The decisions people make in the next 24 to 72 hours could make a real difference in keeping themselves and first responders safe.”
